query: Refractory high-entropy alloys are promising structural materials, but achieving a strong combination of strength and plasticity remains important. What single intervention could improve this strength–plasticity combination? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its expected mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate reference alloy, the conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding controlled amounts of Ti and V to a baseline NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy will improve its strength–plasticity combination by enhancing grain boundary cohesion and providing solute strengthening.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase NbMoTaW refractory HEA exhibiting high-temperature strength but limited room temperature ductility.
generation.intervention: Introducing measured additions of Ti and V into the NbMoTaW alloy composition.
generation.conditions: The alloy is processed under conventional melting and homogenization conditions to obtain a single-phase microstructure; tests are conducted at room temperature for ductility measurements and at high temperatures (e.g., around 1150 °C) for strength evaluations.
generation.structural_mediator: Increased grain boundary cohesion (from Ti addition) and enhanced lattice distortion/solute strengthening (from V addition) that help maintain a stable microstructure.
generation.mechanism: Ti is expected to improve ductility by strengthening the grain boundaries, whereas V contributes to precipitation/hardening mechanisms that boost yield strength; the combined effects lead to a synergistic balance between strength and plasticity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline NbMoTaW alloy, the Ti/V-modified alloy will exhibit a significant improvement in room temperature plasticity (e.g., ductility approaching or exceeding 11.5%) while maintaining or increasing its high-temperature yield strength (with yield strength values meeting or exceeding reported improvements such as a transition from 1058 to around 1246 MPa).
generation.baseline: NbMoTaW refractory HEA without the Ti/V additions.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected as long as the alloy remains a single-phase refractory HEA and the Ti and V contents are within an optimal range; excessive additions that promote secondary brittle phases or phase separation may negate the benefits.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvements in ductility and strength are uncertain due to possible variations in processing conditions and phase stability; the precise optimal concentrations of Ti and V also require further calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: the baseline NbMoTaW alloy and a modified NbMoTaW alloy with carefully controlled additions of Ti and V. Ensure both sets undergo identical processing to obtain a single-phase structure. Perform mechanical testing at room temperature for ductility (measuring compressive/tensile plastic strain) and at high temperatures (around 1150 °C) for yield strength assessment.
measurements: Room temperature ductility (% plastic strain before failure)
Microstructural phase analysis (XRD/SEM) to confirm single-phase structure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti/V-modified alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant increase in room temperature plasticity (targeting around or above 11.5% improvement) and a similar or enhanced high-temperature yield strength compared to the baseline NbMoTaW alloy, or if secondary brittle phases form, then the hypothesis is falsified.

In order to improve plasticity at room temperature (RT), a new refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA), HfNbTaTiZr [], with excellent RT compression plasticity (ε > 50%), has been developed. However, its specific yield strength (SYS) at high temperatures is undesirability (such as <60 MPa·cm3/g at 1073 K). For better SYS, Han et al. [] and Wang et al. [] added Ti or V to NbMoTaW and NbMoTa RHEAs, respectively. Unfortunately, their SYSs are still lower than 90 MPa·cm3/g at 1073 K. Hence, the harmonization of strength, plasticity, and density is an intractable problem in RHEAs. Meanwhile, the strain softening phenomenon in RHEAs at high temperatures is ubiquitous, but the quantitative analysis of the softening mechanism is still lacking [,,,].

One of the most promising and progressive fields in modern material science is high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The first to propose HEAs’ concept was J.W. Yeh [], but since then, it has changed rather significantly, especially during the last few years []. Due to their extremely high mechanical and physical properties, refractory HEAs are classified as a separate group of materials. Such alloying compositions mainly include elements from the IV, V, and VI columns of the periodic table with some additions of Al, Si, Ni, or Co []. First high-entropy equiatomic compositions based on refractory elements, such as NbMoTaW and NbMoTaWV, were obtained in prior research [,]. It was found that the alloys possess higher mechanical properties at higher temperatures in comparison to conventional superalloys, such as Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 []. It was also determined that the addition of V increases the hardness significantly (up to 11.4 GPa at 1150 °C) [] and yield strength σ0.2 from 1058 MPa to 1246 MPa [].
